DISPUTATION ON THE CONTINUATION OF MOTION IN PHYSICS.
Thesis XXXVI.

units.la: {Q}uanquàm motûs distinctio in communem & proprium genuina sit, contingere tamen potest ut qui communis transeat in proprium. Ita quamdiu merces navigio vehuntur, motu moventur communi; Naufragio verò navigium quandò dissilit in fragmenta ut merces seorsim natent, tùnc moventur merces motu proprio, cùm qui communis erat transierit in proprium. Motus sanè, quò merces natant, à communi, quem antea habuerunt, ideò non est distinguendus quia navigium dissiluit impetu vehementiori facto in scopulum, à quo motum merces accepisse dici non potest, cùm quod quiescit motum dare nequeat; ut concludam quòd motus, quò merces post naufragium natant, sit ipse motus, quo ante naufragium vehebantur.
units.tr: Although the distinction of motion into common and proper is genuine, it can nevertheless happen that a motion which is common passes into a proper one. Thus, as long as goods are carried by a ship, they are moved by a common motion; but when, after a shipwreck, the vessel breaks apart into fragments so that the goods float separately, then the goods are moved by a proper motion, since what was common has passed into proper. Indeed, the motion by which the goods float is not to be distinguished from the common motion they had before on the ground that the ship broke apart by a more violent impact against a rock; for the goods cannot be said to have received motion from the rock, since what is at rest cannot give motion. So I conclude that the motion by which the goods float after the shipwreck is the very same motion by which they were carried before the shipwreck.
XXXVII.

units.la: Opponis, Motûs distinctio in communem & proprium æq; relinquit incertum utrum quid moveatur an quiescat ac vulgaris motus descriptio; Contingere enim potest ut quod non movetur motu proprio & sic verè quiescit, moveatur motu communi, quo casu eadem res ex æquo moveri & quiescere dicenda est, quia quod movetur motu communi, non minus verè movetur quàm quod movetur motu proprio. Ita qui sedet in navigio pariter moveri ac quiescere dicendus est, verè enim quiescit habito respectu ad corpora proximè ambientia, verè etiam movetur si spectetur situs, quem sedens in navigio habet inter littora. Resp. 1. Fateor quòd corpus, quod motu movetur communi, verè moveatur; Id quod patet tum ex eo, quia motus communis transire in proprium potest: tum ex eo, quòd sedens in navi fieri in se mutationem sentit quando navis subitò sistitur. 2. Quanquàm quod non movetur motu proprio verè quiescat, & quod motu movetur communi verè moveatur; ut eadem res, docente nostrâ motûs distinctione in communem & proprium, dici subinde possit verè quiescere & verè moveri; incertum tamen distinctio non relinquit, utrum quid moveatur per se nec ne? Motus duntaxat proprius est motus, qui corpori absolutè convenit; Motus verò communis convenit corpori propter aliud; Jam verò incertum esse non potest ex distinctione nostra motûs, utrum quid moveatur motu proprio nec ne? Quia unum & idem corpus non potest uno respectu à corporibus contiguis dici separari, alio verò respectu non separari, sed alterutrum duntaxat locum habet. Ex descriptione verò vulgari motûs incertum etiam relinquitur utrum corpus moveatur nec ne motu quô per se movetur? Cùm loci designatio quælibet in descriptione motûs vulgari æq; pertineat ad motum, quó corpus per se movetur.
units.tr: You object that the distinction of motion into common and proper leaves it equally uncertain whether a thing is moving or at rest, as does the common description of motion. For it can happen that a thing which is not moved by a proper motion, and so is truly at rest, is moved by a common motion; in which case the same thing must be said to move and to rest equally, because what is moved by a common motion is no less truly moved than what is moved by a proper motion. Thus the man who sits in a ship must be said to be both moving and at rest alike: he truly rests with respect to the bodies immediately surrounding him, and he truly moves if one looks at the position he occupies between the shores. Answer: (1) I grant that a body which is moved by a common motion is truly moved; this is clear both from the fact that a common motion can pass into a proper one, and from the fact that a man sitting in a ship feels a change in himself when the ship is suddenly stopped. (2) Although what is not moved by a proper motion truly rests, and what is moved by a common motion is truly moved, so that, according to our distinction of motion into common and proper, the same thing can at times be said to rest truly and to move truly, the distinction nevertheless does not leave it uncertain whether something is moved per se or not. Proper motion alone is the motion which belongs absolutely to a body; common motion belongs to a body on account of something else. Now it cannot be uncertain from our distinction of motion whether something is moved by a proper motion or not, because one and the same body cannot, in one respect, be said to be separated from contiguous bodies and, in another respect, not separated; only one of the two can hold. Moreover, from the common description of motion it likewise remains uncertain whether a body is or is not moved by that motion by which it is moved per se, since any designation of place in the common description of motion pertains equally to the motion by which the body is moved per se.
XXXVIII.

units.la: Quanquàm etiam motus communis corpori non minùs verè quàm proprius conveniat, sufficit tamen Physico illum, qui cuiq; corpori proprius est, considerasse. Tum quia nulli corpori unus duntaxat convenit motus communis; Multitudo autem rerum intricare mentem solet. Tum quia omnes motus communes observari nunquam possunt. Tum deniq; quia omnis motus communis est alicui corpori proprius; & tractari debet ut proprius non verò ut communis, ne committatur ταυτολογία contra sapientiæ legem.
units.tr: Although common motion belongs to a body no less truly than proper motion, it is nevertheless enough for the physicist to have considered that motion which is proper to each body. First, because no body has only one common motion; and the multitude of things is wont to confuse the mind. Second, because all common motions can never be observed. Finally, because every common motion is proper to some body, and it ought to be treated as proper and not as common, lest a tautology be committed against the law of wisdom.
XXXIX.

units.la: Motus proprius multitudine quomodo communis non gaudet, quia uni corpori tantùm convenit unus. Interim considerari proprius potest instar plurium; Ut cùm in rotis currùum duos diversos distinguimus, unum scilicet circularem circa ipsarum axem, alterum secundùm longitudinem viæ per quam feruntur. Sed quòd ideo tales motus non sint revera distincti, patet ex eo, quòd unumquodq; punctum corporis, quod movetur, unam tantùm lineam describit. Vel absidi à latere infigatur baculus, & currus ab equis protrahatur ut circa axem rota se circumvolvat, & patebit oculis quòd baculus unam duntaxat describit lineam, quæ arcuata erit.
units.tr: A proper motion does not enjoy multiplicity as a common motion does, because only one motion belongs to one body. Nevertheless, a proper motion can be considered as if it were several; as when, in the wheels of carriages, we distinguish two different motions, namely one circular about their axle, and another along the length of the road on which they are carried. But that such motions are not really distinct is clear from the fact that each point of the moving body describes only one line. Let a staff be fixed to the side of a wheel and the carriage be drawn by horses so that the wheel turns about its axle; it will be plain to the eye that the staff describes only one line, and that this line is curved.
XL.

units.la: Nec refert quòd linea sæpè sit valdè contorta, & ideò ex pluribus diversis motibus genita videatur, quia possumus imaginari eodem modo quamcunq; lineam etiam rectam, quæ omnium simplicissima est, ex indefinitis diversis motibus ortam esse. Ut si linea A.B. feratur versus C.D. & eodem tempore punctum A. feratur versus B. linea recta A.D. quam hoc punctum A. describet, non minus pendet à duobus motibus rectis ab A. in B. & ab A.B. in C.D. quàm linea curva, quæ à quovis rotæ puncto describitur, pendet à motu recto & circulari. Talis linea describitur à motu pilæ plumbeæ, quam multi viri docti ferunt è summo malo in navem velocissimè provectam ad mali pedem ad perpendiculum decidere. Ubi quanquàm pilæ motus ex duobus, scil. ex progressivo & descensorio videatur compositus, revera tamen unus tantùm est & quidem rectus. Et oritur partim à vi gravitatis, partim à determinatione motûs, quem cum navigio, antequàm inceperit decidere, communem habuit; ut qui communis erat, nunc transierit in proprium. Quanquàm & aër prorsùm agitatus motum progressivum quoq; juvet. Itaq; quamvis ex illo præcepto methodi, quò jubemur difficultates, quas examinaturi sumus, in tot partes dividere, quot expedit ad illas commodiùs resolvendas, perspæpè quidem utile sit, unum motum in plures partes dictò modò distinguere ad faciliorem ejus intelligentiam comparandam, absolutè tamen loquendo unus tantùm in unoquoq; corpore motus est, qui ei proprius.
units.tr: Nor does it matter that the line is often very twisted, and therefore seems to have been produced from several different motions, because we can imagine in the same way that any line, even a straight one, which is the simplest of all, has arisen from an indefinite number of different motions. For example, if the line AB is carried toward CD, and at the same time the point A is carried toward B, the straight line AD which this point A describes depends no less upon the two straight motions, from A to B and from AB to CD, than a curved line described by any point of a wheel depends upon a straight and a circular motion. Such a line is described by the motion of a leaden ball, which many learned men report falls perpendicularly to the foot of the mast from the top of the mast of a ship carried very swiftly forward. Here, although the motion of the ball seems to be compounded of two, namely of the progressive and of the downward motion, in truth it is only one, and indeed straight. It arises partly from the force of gravity, partly from the direction of the motion which it had in common with the ship before it began to fall; so that what was common has now passed into proper. Although the air, driven forward, also aids the forward motion. Therefore, although it is often quite useful, in accordance with that rule of method by which we are bidden to divide the difficulties we are about to examine into as many parts as is convenient for resolving them more easily, to distinguish one motion into several parts in the manner described, in order to make it easier to grasp, nevertheless, speaking absolutely, there is only one motion in each body, and it is the proper one.
XLI.

units.la: Hodiè tantundem est motùs quantum fuit ab initio. Sol enim, siquidem moveatur, æq; celeriter hodiè currit ac ab initio. Deinde cur pila, quæ murum impetit, motum retinet nisi quia non communicavit? Unde concludendum quòd motus in corpore non pereat nisi communicatione. Et nisi certi termini motui essent positi, citra metam adaugeri vel minui posset; Unde fieret ut vel in unam flammam vel in rigorem abirent omnia. Deniq; rationi maximè est consentaneum, ut quantum motùs Deus primitùs produxit, tantundem conservet; Cùm id constantia & immutabilitas Dei requirere videatur: Quemadmodum enim constantia & immutabilitas Dei causa est cur tantundem materiæ conservet quantum initiò produxit; Ita eadem Dei constantia requirit, ut quantum motûs in rerum primordio produxit tantundem quoq; conservet. Cujus comparationis necessitas nititur consideratione, quâ & conservationem continuatam esse creationem & motum non minus præcariò in materia quàm materiam in universo extare intelligimus.
units.tr: Today there is exactly as much motion as there was at the beginning. For the sun, if indeed it moves, runs today just as swiftly as it did from the beginning. Again, why does a ball that strikes a wall retain its motion, unless it has not communicated it? Hence it must be concluded that motion in a body does not perish except by communication. And unless fixed limits had been set for motion, it could be increased or diminished without measure; whence it would follow that all things would pass either into one flame or into rigid stillness. Finally, it is most consonant with reason that God preserves as much motion as He first produced; since this seems to be required by the constancy and immutability of God. For just as the constancy and immutability of God is the cause why He preserves as much matter as He produced at the beginning, so the same constancy of God requires that He also preserve as much motion as He produced at the origin of things. The necessity of this comparison rests on the consideration by which we understand that continued conservation is creation, and that motion exists in matter no less precariously than matter exists in the universe.
XLII.

units.la: Adeò verum est quòd hodiè tantundem sit motûs quantum fuit initiò, ut ne Angeli novum condere motum possint, quandò enim corpora movent utuntur motu qui in rerum natura jam est, eò fere modò quò anima suum movet corpus: Atqui anima suum corpus movet non condendo novum motum, sed motum, qui in corpore jam est, infleƈtendo; Quomodo auriga, qui currui insidet, nec currui nec equis motum dat, sed motum, qui & in curru & in equis jam est, pro arbitrio regit. Et certè satis motûs in rerum natura Angeli inveniunt, quò vel maxima corpora concutere & prosternere possint, ut necesse non sit novum ab ipsis condi motum. Quæris quomodò motum Angeli copulare & ad corpora permovenda accommodare soleant? Resp. Motum Angeli dirigunt quomodo anima nostra motum spirituum animalium; Anima nostra spiritus animales, qui in corpore nostro sunt, huc illuc flecƈtit solâ voluntate; Sive enim ambulare sive stare sive sedere, &c. velim, illico spiritus animales corpus vel ad ambulandum propellunt vel ad standum erigunt vel ad sessionem incurvant. Haud dubiè modus, quo anima nostra corpora movet, non est nobilior modò quò Angeli corpora movent, cùm Angeli præstantiores res sint creaturæ quàm sit anima nostra. Et si ex unione, quâ anima corpori est unita, sequi videtur quòd anima in suo corpore aliâ ratione operetur quàm Angeli in corporibus quæ movent, sciendum est quòd anima corpori suo ideò dicatur unita, quia illud solâ voluntate movere potest; Ut Angeli corporibus quæ movent, etiam uniti sint dicendi, quia ea solâ voluntate movent. Magna interim est differentia inter unionē Angeli cum corpore & unionem animæ nostræ cum corpore suo: Anima enim non tantùm corpori est unita, sed etiam vice versâ corpus unitum est animæ, dum corpus in animam vicissim agere potest varios in ea excitando sensus; Angeli vero corporibus uniri solent, non verò vicissim; Quamquam enim corpora Angeli moveant, corpora tamen in Angelos nunquam agunt.
units.tr: It is so true that today there is as much motion as there was at the beginning, that angels cannot even create new motion. For when they move bodies, they use a motion that already exists in the nature of things, very much in the way that the soul moves its body. Yet the soul moves its body not by creating a new motion, but by bending the motion that already is in the body; just as a charioteer who sits on the chariot gives motion neither to the chariot nor to the horses, but directs at will the motion that is already both in the chariot and in the horses. And certainly angels find enough motion in the nature of things, by which they can shake and overthrow even the very greatest bodies, so that there is no need for them to create new motion. You ask how angels are accustomed to join motion and adapt it to moving bodies? I answer: they direct motion in the way our soul directs the motion of the animal spirits. Our soul bends the animal spirits, which are in our body, this way and that by the will alone; for whether I wish to walk, stand or sit, etc., at once the animal spirits drive the body either to walking, or raise it to standing, or bend it into sitting. Without doubt, the manner in which our soul moves bodies is no nobler than the manner in which angels move bodies, since angels are more excellent beings than our soul is. And if it seems to follow from the union by which the soul is united to the body that the soul works in its own body by a different method from that by which angels work in the bodies they move, it must be known that the soul is said to be united to its body because it can move it by the will alone; so angels too are to be said to be united to the bodies they move, because they move them by the will alone. Meanwhile there is a great difference between the union of an angel with a body and the union of our soul with its body. For the soul is not only united to the body, but conversely the body is also united to the soul, since the body can in turn act upon the soul by arousing various sensations in it; whereas angels are wont to be united to bodies, but not conversely. For although angels move bodies, bodies never act upon angels.
XLIII.

units.la: Objicis Primò: Motus est tantùm modus, proinde nulla est necessitas ut quantum motûs fuit ab initio etiamnùm tantundem sit; Nisi simul dicere velimus, quòd hodiè tantundem sit figuræ, sitûs, magnitudinis & quietis, quantum fuit initiò: Quod posterius falsum est. Resp. α. Hodiè omninò tantundem est quietis quantum fuit initiò. β. Magna est differentia inter motum & reliquos modos, motus enim in materia est gratuitò, reliqui autem modi sunt motûs effecta.
units.tr: You object, first: motion is only a mode; therefore there is no necessity that as much motion as there was at the beginning should still be the same amount. Unless we wish to say at the same time that today there is as much figure, position, magnitude and rest as there was at the beginning, which latter is false. I answer: (a) today there is exactly as much rest as there was at the beginning. (b) There is a great difference between motion and the other modes; for motion in matter is not a result of something else, whereas the other modes are effects of motion.
XLIV.

units.la: Objicis Secundò: Contingere potest ut pila plumbea excussa tormento bellico impingat in clavos erectos & muro firmiter infixos, quo casu pilæ motus peribit absq; concussione clavorum vel muri, proinde periit absq; communicatione. Resp. Quia pila plumbea motum nec muro nec clavis communicat propter vehementiorem eorum resistentiam, motum pilæ recipit aër, qui inde ita celeriter agitatur, ut vehemens edatur strepitus.
units.tr: You object, second: it can happen that a leaden ball, fired from a war engine, strikes upright nails firmly fixed in a wall; in that case the motion of the ball perishes without any shaking of the nails or the wall, and therefore it perishes without communication. I answer: because the leaden ball communicates its motion neither to the wall nor to the nails, on account of their greater resistance, the air receives the motion of the ball, and is thereby agitated so swiftly that a loud noise is produced.
XLV.

units.la: Objicis Tertiò: Nunquid novi motûs productionem probat animalium antea quiescentium incessus, volatus, reptatio, natatio? Resp. Motus spirituum in animalibus, dum moventur, transit in alias eorum partes, ut spiritus, qui promiscuè antea movebantur, nunc in certa membra motum determinatum habeant: Ut res se habeat quomodo in aqua, quæ quamdiu stagnans est, quiescere videtur, cùm particulæ ejus exiguæ moveantur motu promiscuo, postea verò quando aqua fluere incipit, aquæ particulæ motum promiscuum mutant determinatæ versus unam regionem. Et quantum motûs in animalibus, quæ movetur, accedit membris, tantum spiritibus animalibus decedit. Instas. Quando mercenarius toto laborat die, brachia tam frequenter movet, ut quantum motûs brachiis accessit, tantundè spiritibus decessisse non videatur, quin omnes omninò spiritus vesperi sint exhausti. Resp. a. Spiritibus multum decessisse motûs ex labore testis est lassitudo. b. Sciendum quòd spiritibus animalibus summa motûs sit celeritas, ut in iis plurimum motûs resideat; Brachiorum verò mercenarij motûs tarditas admodùm est magna quandò comparatio fit cum motu spirituum animalium: Ut mirum non sit, quòd spiritus animales totâ die brachiis motum comunicare possunt.
units.tr: You object, third: does not the walking, flying, creeping and swimming of animals that were previously at rest prove the production of new motion? I answer: the motion of the spirits in animals, while they are moving, passes into their other parts, so that spirits which previously moved in a random way now have a determinate motion in certain members. The matter is like that of water, which while it stands still seems to be at rest, though its tiny particles move with a random motion; but afterwards, when the water begins to flow, the particles of the water change their random motion into one directed toward a single region. And as much motion as is added to the limbs of an animal that is moving, so much is taken away from the animal spirits. Objection continued. When a hired labourer works all day, he moves his arms so often that it does not seem that as much motion as was added to the arms has been taken from the spirits, so that all the spirits are altogether exhausted by evening. I answer: (a) that the spirits have lost much motion through labour is attested by weariness. (b) It must be known that the animal spirits have the highest speed of motion, so that most of the motion resides in them; whereas the motion of the labourer's arms is very slow when compared with the motion of the animal spirits. So it is no wonder that the animal spirits can communicate motion to the arms throughout the whole day.
XLVI.

units.la: Objicis Quartò: Alicujus motûs interitum arguit pila magnâ vi in arenæ cumulum conjecta, cujus motus cessante arenæ tremore totus periisse videtur. Resp. Pilæ in arenam conjectæ motus primò transfertur in ipsam arenam, unde arenæ tremor; Ac deinde sic in aërem transfertur ut oculis non magis cerni possit quàm ipse aër: Nihil enim est quod motum facilius recipiat quàm aër, idq; exinde est quòd aër divisus est in particulas admodùm exiguas, quæ singulæ motum jam habent.
units.tr: You object fourthly: the motion of a ball hurled with great force into a heap of sand proves that some motion has perished, since when the tremor of the sand ceases the whole motion seems to have vanished. Reply: the motion of the ball thrown into the sand is first transferred to the sand itself, whence the tremor of the sand; and then it is so transferred into the air that it can no more be seen by the eyes than the air itself. For there is nothing that receives motion more easily than air, and this is because the air is divided into very small particles, each of which already has motion.
XLVII.

units.la: Objicis Quintò: Fragor, qui excitatur quoties tormentum bellicum exploditur, non nisi ad certum aliquod spatium se diffundit, & non nisi per breve tempus sentitur, cùm paulò post iterum cesset, ut videatur evidentissimè sequi illò saltem tempore, quò perstrepebat tormentum, fuisse plus motûs in mundo quàm fuerit antè. Resp. Sensibus in hoc negotio non tantoperè est fidendum, cùm nos in re prorsus simili jam à pueris fefellerint; Dum enim luculentus instruitur ignis, qui priùs non apparebat, existimamus novum aliquod corpus in orbe existere; Cùmque flamma extinguitur, putamus eam desinere, quoniam ex oculis nostris abit; Quanquam vacui maxima absurditas ignem non in nihilum abiisse probet.
units.tr: You object fifthly: the crash that is produced whenever a piece of artillery is fired spreads only over a certain distance and is felt only for a short time, since it soon ceases again; so it seems most evidently to follow that, at least during the time when the artillery was roaring, there was more motion in the world than there was before. Reply: we must not put too much trust in the senses in this matter, since they have deceived us in a wholly similar case from childhood. For when a bright fire is kindled which was not visible before, we think some new body has come into existence in the world; and when the flame is put out, we suppose it ceases to be, because it leaves our eyes; yet the enormous absurdity of a void does not prove that the fire has gone into nothing.
XLVIII.

units.la: Etiam omnis motus est circularis, quia aliàs motus nullus fieret. Quemvis alium quàm circularem fieri finge & repeires eum absq; corporum penetratione vel vacui absurditate contingere non posse. Motus proinde omnis est circularis, hoc est, dum corpus aliquod locò movetur, illud eòdem temporis momentò pellit aliud, hociterum impellit aliud & aliud, usq; ad ultimum: quod cùm, ob omnium aliorum locorum plenitudinem, alium locum non inveniat quàm illum, quem corpus primò motum reliquit, hoc ultimum in primi locum necessario. fiò venit. Ita si cubiculum fit clausum, ut tubus camini, per quem fumus exit, à latere foramine hiet, sentietur continuò magnus ventus, qui per hoc foramen ad focum tendit. Ita quantum ex dolio vini effluit, tantundem è vestigio aëris dolium ingreditur. Quid quòd & Luna & Planetæ omnes motus circulares habent? Ut vel eorum exemplo nos natura docere videatur, quòd omnis motus sit circularis.
units.tr: Also every motion is circular, for otherwise no motion would take place. Imagine any motion other than circular, and you will find that it cannot occur without the penetration of bodies or the absurdity of a void. Therefore every motion is circular: that is, while one body is moved from its place, at the same instant it pushes another, this in turn pushes another and another, up to the last; and since, because of the fullness of all other places, this last body finds no other place than that which the body first moved has left, it necessarily comes into the place of the first. So if a room is closed except for a hole at the side, like the flue of a chimney through which smoke escapes, a great wind will be felt continually, blowing through this hole towards the hearth. So as much air immediately enters a cask of wine as flows out of it. And what of the fact that the Moon and all the planets have circular motions? So that from their example nature itself seems to teach us that every motion is circular.
XLIX.

units.la: Nec putandum est quòd circulus motûs semper sit perfectus: Sufficit si motus desinat ibi, unde incepit.
units.tr: Nor is it to be thought that the circle of motion is always perfect: it is enough if the motion ends where it began.
L.

units.la: Nec etiam existimandum est quòd quicquid movetur, moveatur circulariter. Mensa enim, quæ à fenestris movetur ad januam, non habet motum circularem, cùm non redeat eòdem unde incepit moveri. Distingue ergò phrases: Omne corpus quod movetur, movetur circulariter. Nullus sit motus, quin integer motûs fiat circulus. Prior phrasis falsa est, ut id ex mensæ exemplo patet. Posterior verò vera est ubiquè. Ita quanquàm mensa, quando à fenestris propellitur versùs januam, non circulariter moveatur, circulus tamen motûs contingit, & quidem singulis momentis, ita ut in mensæ motu innumeri contingant circuli; Nullò enim momento movetur mensa, quin ei aliquid aëris & cedat & succedat.
units.tr: Nor again should it be supposed that whatever is moved is moved in a circle. For a table which is pushed from the windows towards the door does not have a circular motion, since it does not return to the place from which it began to move. Distinguish therefore the propositions: "Every body which is moved is moved circularly"; "No motion occurs without a complete circle of motion being made." The former is false, as the example of the table makes plain; the latter is true everywhere. So although the table, when it is propelled from the windows towards the door, is not moved circularly, nevertheless a circle of motion occurs, and indeed at every instant, so that in the motion of the table countless circles occur; for the table is never moved at any moment without some air both yielding to it and rushing in behind it.
LI.

units.la: Circulus etiam integer eòdem movetur momento, ut eòdem temporis momento, quò unum corpus incipit moveri, omnia reliqua corpora, quæ circulum componunt, moveantur; Idq; verum est quantumvis evagetur circulus. Nisi enim eòdem tempore integer moveretur circulus, daretur corporis penetratio vel vacuum. Ita eòdem eodem momento, quo vinum e dolio effluit, aeris aliquid per foramen aliud dolium ingreditur.
units.tr: Also a whole circle is moved in the same instant, so that in the same moment in which one body begins to move, all the other bodies which make up the circle are moved; and this is true however far the circle extends. For if the whole circle were not moved at the same time, there would be penetration of bodies or a void. So at the very same moment in which the wine flows out of the cask, some air enters another cask through a different hole.
LII.

units.la: Nec propterea circulus movebitur momento: Aliud enim est motum esse momentaneum: Aliud vero motum transmitti in momento. Quanquam enim motus successive contingat, in momento tamen transmitti potest. Ita quando baculus movetur, ab una extremitate transfibit motus in momento ad alteram, ut omnes baculi partes eodem moveantur momento, quanquam interim baculus successive moveatur.
units.tr: Nor on that account will the circle be moved in a moment: "For it is one thing for a motion to be momentary; it is another for a motion to be transmitted in a moment." Although motion occurs successively, it can nevertheless be transmitted in a moment. Thus when a staff is moved, the motion passes in a moment from one end to the other, so that all parts of the staff are moved in the same moment, although meanwhile the staff is moved successively.
LIII.

units.la: Proinde nihil incipit moveri, quin integrum circulum movere possit; Ut etiam pulviculi singuli, quos in sole volantes perspicimus, suos pellant circulos: Ut inde quam fluxa & mobilis aeris materia videre fit. Nec necesse est a corpore, unde circulus incipit, circulo integrum impertiri motum; Quando enim circulus in fluido contingere debet, vis quantumvis exigua sufficit ad inchoandum & absolvendum circulum, fluidi enim particulae jam habent motum, qui est quaquaversus, ut eas quivis aliunde adveniens motus determinare possit.
units.tr: Therefore nothing begins to move without being able to move a whole circle; just as the individual specks of dust which we see flying in the sunlight each drive their own circles, whence it is seen how fluid and mobile the matter of the air is. Nor is it necessary that the whole circular motion be imparted by the body from which the circle begins; for when a circle is to occur in a fluid, however small a force suffices to begin and complete the circle, since the particles of the fluid already have motion, which runs in every direction, so that any motion arriving from elsewhere can determine them.
LIV.

units.la: Adeo verum est quod omnis motus sit circularis, ut si circulus impediatur, nullus fiat motus; Ita ex dolio nulla effluet guttula neq; ex ampulla inversa quamdiu aer dolium vel ampullam ingredi non potest. Imo nec Angeli impedire motum circularem possunt, quia nititur plenitudine corporum, ut nisi vel vacuum vel corporum penetratio fiat, alius motus quam circularis fieri nequeat: Atqui Angeli neutrum efficere possunt. Etiam Homines aquis tutò inambularent, quandò circulus impediri posset.
units.tr: So true is it that all motion is circular, that if the circle is hindered, no motion takes place. Thus no drop flows out of a cask, nor out of an inverted flask, as long as air cannot enter the cask or flask. Indeed, not even angels can impede circular motion, since it depends on the fullness of bodies, so that unless either a vacuum or a penetration of bodies takes place, a motion other than circular cannot occur. But angels can do neither. Men too could walk safely on the waters, whenever the circle could be hindered.
LV.

units.la: Præterea omnis omninò motus fit abimpulsu; Ut & vim tractricem naturæ denegemus omnem & fugam vacui, quò suam vulgò Physicam implent, & naturam, ut pulsionem fictâ terrent larvâ, fugacem faciunt, dericulo habeamus. Ita quando ex hydria per calamum bibunt aquam, aqua ascendit impulsa; Venter enim bibentis sese primò distenditur inde aër propellatur, qui ingreditur hydriam aquamq; premit ut propellatur in calamum & os bibentis ingrediatur: Quia aër alium locum, in quem recedat, non invenit, ob resistentiam omnium aliorum corporum: Itâ cucurbitulæ contrahunt cutem impulsu, dum enim ignis aërem ex cucurbitula expellit, condensatur aër extra cucurbitulam, qui æthere intercurrente conatur sese dilatare, quò conatu premit æqualiter cutem, unde sanguis provocatur. Ita in thermometro contingit ut quando aër externus majorem calorem est adeptus, internum, qui thermometro est inclusus, dilatet; quâ dilatatione superficies aquæ fortis premitur, ut proratione dilatationis magis vel minus alte deprimatur.
units.tr: Moreover, all motion whatsoever arises from impulsion. So we deny the attractive power of nature altogether, and the flight from a vacuum, by which the common Physics fill up their pages; they frighten us with the phantom of nature's pushing and make it a fleeting thing, so that we may have an example. Thus when people drink water from a jug through a straw, the water rises by impulsion: the belly of the drinker first distends, and the air is driven out from there; this air enters the jug and presses on the water so that it is propelled into the straw and enters the mouth of the drinker. For the air finds no other place to retreat into, because of the resistance of all the other bodies. Likewise cupping-glasses draw up the skin by impulsion: when the fire expels the air from the cupping-glass, the air outside the glass is condensed, and, with the ether intervening, it tries to expand; by this effort it presses the skin equally, and so the blood is drawn out. Again, in the thermometer it happens that when the external air has acquired greater heat, it expands the internal air enclosed in the thermometer; by this expansion the surface of the strong water is pressed down, and it is depressed more or less deeply in proportion to the expansion.

units.la: Si verò contingat ut aër externus frigidior factus sit, aër, qui thermometro est inclusus, inde quoq; refrigeratur; Hinc aër externus gravior factus premit aquam fortem in vasculo contentam ut ascendat, ascensus etiam juvatur quòd aër, qui thermometro inclusus, refrigeratus ad angustius spatium redigitur. Thermometri usus apprimè facit ad tempestatis variationem observandam, caloris scil. & frigoris mutatos gradus: Ut qui tempore hyemali juvare plantarum germinationem volentes hypocausta certò temperamentò calefaciunt, thermometri ope utilissimè uti possint.
units.tr: But if, on the other hand, the external air becomes colder, the air enclosed in the thermometer is cooled as well; hence the external air, now heavier, presses the strong water contained in the little vessel so that it rises, and the rise is also helped because the air enclosed in the thermometer, being cooled, is drawn into a narrower space. The use of the thermometer is especially serviceable for observing changes in the weather, namely the varying degrees of heat and cold; so those who, in winter, wishing to help the germination of plants, warm their hothouses with a certain moderate heat, may use the thermometer to very great advantage.
LVI.

units.la: Ut verò circulus locum ubivis habeat oportet locorum inæqualitates compensari inæqualitate motûs, hoc est, quò locus, quem circulus transit, spatiosior vel angustior, eò motus tardior vel celerior est. Ponamus E. G. locos tres, quorum secundus duplo sit angustior primô, & tertius quadruplo angustior eòdem primô, necessum erit ut materia eadem duplo celerius moveatur in loco secundo & quadruplo celerius in loco tertio, quàm in primo mota fuit. Hacq; ratione si celeritas motûs angustiam loci ubiq; penset & æquet, eôdem tempore per angustiorem locum non minus materiæ transit quàm per laxiorem; Ita ut minimè necesse sit aut vacuum comminisci, aut condensationem materiæ admittere.
units.tr: But so that the circulation may hold good everywhere, the inequalities of places must be balanced by an inequality of motion: that is, the narrower or wider the space the circulation passes through, the slower or faster the motion. Let us suppose, for example, three places, of which the second is twice as narrow as the first and the third four times as narrow as the same first place. It will necessarily follow that the same matter moves twice as fast in the second place and four times as fast in the third as it moved in the first. In this way, if the speed of the motion everywhere weighs and matches the narrowness of the place, then in the same time no less matter passes through the narrower place than through the wider one; so that there is no need at all either to devise a vacuum or to admit a condensation of matter.
LVII.

units.la: Hujusce compensationis quotidiana habemus exempla; Ita videmus aquam fluvij per patentem alveum tardo provehi motu, per angustias verò celerrimè abripi. Sic aër ex folle, quamvis lente claudatur, valdè tamen celeriter egreditur propter foraminis angustiam.
units.tr: We have daily examples of this compensation: we see the water of a river flow slowly along a broad channel, but rush swiftly through narrows. So air from a bellows, although the nozzle is closed slowly, nevertheless escapes quite quickly on account of the narrowness of the opening.
LVIII.

units.la: Quæris, unde motûs celeritas in angustioribus locis & ejusdem motûs tarditas in patentioribus oriatur? Resp. Fluidum quodvis habet promiscuum particularum suarum motum; Hic motus ex parte transire solet in fluxum quando fluidum fluit; Ut nova sic fiat motûs determinatio. Et fluidum nunquàm tam celeriter fluit quin in eo motûs promiscui multùm superfit; Quò celerior verò est fluxus, eò debilior est motus promiscuus, & quò fluxus tardior, eò motus quoq; promiscuus est celerior. Proinde celeritas fluidi in angustioribus locis oritur ex diminutione motûs promiscui; Tarditas verò fluxûs in patentioribus locis oritur ex motûs promiscui incremento. Ita ut neq; in angustioribus neq; in patentioribus locis novus fiat motus, sed nova duntaxat motûs determinatio.
units.tr: You ask: whence arises the speed of motion in narrower places, and the slowness of the same motion in wider ones? I answer: every fluid has a random motion of its own particles. This motion usually passes in part into flow when the fluid flows, so that a new determination of motion arises. A fluid never flows so swiftly that a great deal of random motion does not remain in it. The swifter the flow, the weaker the random motion; and the slower the flow, the faster the random motion. Therefore the speed of a fluid in narrower places arises from a diminution of random motion, while the slowness of the flow in wider places arises from an increase of random motion. Thus in neither narrower nor wider places does a new motion arise, but only a new determination of motion.
LIX.

units.la: Ex eo, quòd in omni motu integer simul movetur circulus, sequitur materiam esse divisam in indefinitum, hoc est, in tot partes, ut nullam cogitatione determinare possimus tam exiguam, quin intelligamus ipsam in alias minores reipsa esse divisam. Finge enim materiam, quæ primò unum duntaxat implevit circuli spatium, deinde implere successive spatia ejusdem circuli innumeris gradibus minora & minora & reperies id fieri non posse, quin materia, quæ primò majus circuli spatium implevit, divisa fit in indefinitum. Primò enim materia circuli spatia innumeris gradibus minora & minora transfire non potest, quin materiæ innumerâ varietate minor minorq; fiat diminutio. Secundò tanta spatiorum minorum minorumq; varietas innumerabili angulorum diversitate est terminata, quos omnes eadem materia successive implere non potest, quinad innumerabiles eorum mensuras innumerabiles accomodet figuras, ut quantulacunq; angulorum spatiola aptè impleantur. Quod ut fiat necesse est omnes imaginabiles materiæ particulas, quæ sunt revera innumeræ, à se mutuò aliquantulum removeri; Eædem enim materiæ particulæ, quæ unius anguli extrema spatiola impleverunt, non sunt aptæ ut proximè subsequentis anguli extremitates impleant, unde necesse est alias materiæ particulas ad occupandum accedere, & quæ particulæ extremitates superioris anguli occupárunt, nunc mediam particularum turbam sunt ingressæ, quam etiam ingressæ non sunt, quin aliæ particulæ earum figuræ se accomodaverint quàm antea; Hæcq; ordinis inter materiæ particulas mutatio innumerâ varietate fieri debet, quia in circulo, de quo dictum, innumeram angulorum varietatem occupare debent; Et talis quantulacunq; innumerâ varietate particularum â se mutuò factaremotio vera est materiæin indefinitum divisio.
units.tr: From the fact that in all motion a whole circle is moved at once, it follows that matter is divided into the indefinite, that is, into so many parts that we cannot by thought determine any part so small that we do not understand it to be actually divided into still smaller ones. For imagine matter which at first filled only a single space of the circle, and then successively fills spaces of the same circle smaller and smaller by innumerable degrees; you will find that this cannot happen unless the matter which first filled the larger space of the circle is divided into the indefinite. First, matter cannot pass through spaces of the circle smaller and smaller by innumerable degrees without a diminution of the matter, smaller and smaller, through an innumerable variety. Second, so great a variety of smaller and smaller spaces is bounded by an innumerable diversity of angles, all of which the same matter cannot successively fill, unless it adapts itself to innumerable measures of them by innumerable shapes, so that even the smallest little spaces of the angles are fitly filled. To bring this about it is necessary that all imaginable particles of matter, which are in truth innumerable, be removed a little from one another. For the same particles of matter which filled the extreme little spaces of one angle are not fit to fill the extremities of the next angle; hence it is necessary that other particles approach to occupy them, and the particles which occupied the extremities of the higher angle now enter the middle crowd of particles, which they would not have entered unless other particles had adapted their shapes differently than before. This change in the order among the particles of matter must take place in an innumerable variety, because in the circle of which we speak they must occupy an innumerable variety of angles. And such a removal, however small, of particles from one another through an innumerable variety is the true division of matter into the indefinite.
LX.

units.la: Interim notandum est nos non loqui de tota materia, sed tantùm de aliqua ejus parte. Fieri enim potest in maximo circuli spatio duas aut tres esse materiæ partes tantæ latitudinis quantæ est angustissimum circuli spatium, quas circulariter per integrum circulum moveri posse facilè intelligimus quanquàm in indefinitum non sint divisæ & solam celeritatem motûs ad rationem loci occupandi accomodent. Interim majores illæ materiæ partes in circulo moveri non possent nisi aliæ multòq; minores ipsis admistæ essent, quæ se quomodolibet inflectant & figuras suas sic mutent, ut junctæ istis majoribus figuras suas non ita mutantibus sed solam celeritatem motûs ad rationem loci occupandi accommodantibus, omnes angulos, quos istæ majores non occupant, accuratè compleant.
units.tr: Meanwhile it must be noted that we are not speaking of the whole of matter, but only of some part of it. For it may happen that in the largest space of the circle there are two or three parts of matter of a breadth equal to the narrowest space of the circle, which we easily understand can be moved circularly through the whole circle, although they are not divided into the indefinite, and which adapt only their speed of motion to the proportion of the place to be occupied. Meanwhile those larger parts of matter could not be moved in the circle unless much smaller parts were mixed with them, which bend in whatever way and so change their shapes that, joined to those larger parts which do not change their shapes in this way but only adapt their speed of motion to the proportion of the place to be occupied, they exactly fill all the angles which those larger parts do not occupy.
LXI.

units.la: Et quamvis quomodo fiat indefinita materiæ divisio cogitatione comprehendere nequeamus, non ideò tamen dubitare debemus quin fiat; Quia clarè percipimus illam necessariò sequi ex natura materiæ nobis evidentissimè cognita, percipimusq; etiam eam esse de genere mere eorum, quæ â mente nostra, quia finita est, capi non possunt. Finge enim particulam materiæ quatumvis exiguam & reperies eam porrò dividi posse quia suis constat portiunculis: Sume easdem portiunculas & reperies eas porrò dividi posse, & ita deinceps. Ut tandem fatearis necesse sit divisionem materiæ nobis esse incomprehensibilem, quia eam nobis incomprehensibilem esse clarè percipimus.
units.tr: And although we cannot grasp by thought how the indefinite division of matter comes about, we ought nevertheless not to doubt that it does; for we clearly perceive that it necessarily follows from the nature of matter, which is most evidently known to us, and we also perceive that it is of the kind that belongs purely to those things which cannot be grasped by our mind, because it is finite. For imagine a particle of matter however small, and you will find that it can be divided further, since it consists of its own little portions. Take those same little portions, and you will find that they too can be divided further, and so on. So at last you must confess that the division of matter is incomprehensible to us, because we clearly perceive that it is incomprehensible to us.
LXII.

units.la: Et sanè Aristotelici fluidum ita considerant, ut, quanquàm materiam in indefinitum revera divisam esse non dixerint, inde sequatur in indefinitum materiam revera divisam esse. Considerarunt enim Aristotelici fluidum ita ut dixerint de fluidis, quòd alienis terminis facilè se accommodent; Id quod fieri non posse suprà demonstravimus, quin materia in indefinitum sit divisa. Interim observari volumus quòd materiæ divisio in indefinitum non cadat in quodvis fluidum, sed in eam duntaxat materiæ partem, quæ à nobis materia primi elementi vocatur.
units.tr: And indeed the Aristotelians consider fluid in such a way that, although they did not say that matter is in truth divided into the indefinite, it follows from their view that matter is in truth divided into the indefinite. For the Aristotelians considered fluid in such a way that, as they said of fluids, they readily adapt themselves to foreign boundaries; and we have shown above that this cannot happen unless matter is divided into the indefinite. Meanwhile we wish it to be observed that the division of matter into the indefinite does not apply to every fluid, but only to that part of matter which by us is called the matter of the first element.
LXIII.

units.la: Nullus etiam motus tàm velox est quin intelligamus clarè & distinctè quòd velocior esse possit; Ita ut affirmemus motum augeri in indefinitum posse. Ut argumentum Copernicanorum, quô firmamenti raptum destruere volunt, nullius sit conatis quando ita argumentantur; Si firmamentum moveretur, singulæ stellæ fixæ motu horario absolverent, secundùm computationem Tychonianam, milliaria 26277. Quæ motûs celeritas, inquiunt, absurda est, quia eam nobis imaginari non possumus. Argumentum nihili facimus quia clarè & distinctè intelligimus quòd motus augeri in indefinitum possit, ita ut statuendum quòd motus innumeris gradibus velocior efse possit. In accurata veri inquisitione non attendendum quid nobis imaginari, sed quid clarè & distinctè intelligere possimus. Chiliogonum etiam nobis imaginari non possumus, an propterea negandum quòd constet mille angulis? Satis est clarè & distinctè intelligi quòd mille angulis constet.
units.tr: No motion is so swift that we cannot clearly and distinctly understand that it could be swifter, so we may affirm that motion can be increased without limit. The argument of the Copernicans, by which they wish to destroy the rapid motion of the firmament, has no force when they argue thus: if the firmament were moving, each fixed star would complete its hourly course at 26,277 miles according to the Tychonic computation; this speed, they say, is absurd because we cannot imagine it. We make nothing of this argument, because we clearly and distinctly understand that motion can be increased without limit, so that it must be granted that motion could be swifter by innumerable degrees. In a careful inquiry into truth, we must attend not to what we can imagine but to what we can clearly and distinctly understand. We cannot imagine a chiliogon either; should we therefore deny that it has a thousand angles? It is enough to understand clearly and distinctly that it has a thousand angles.
LXIV.

units.la: Quàm sensus cæcutiant in subtiliore veri indagatione patet vel ex exemplo motûs. Fieri enim potest ut quòd in velocissimo est motu id quiescere visus judicet; Sic lapis molaris in gyrum vehementer circumactus quiescere visui videtur. Ita in navigio sedentes, quanquàm navigium velocissimè provehatur, facilè contingit judicare navigium quiescere.
units.tr: How blind the senses are in the finer investigation of truth is evident even from the example of motion. For it can happen that the sense judges to be at rest what is in the swiftest motion. Thus a millstone turned violently in a circle seems at rest to the eye. Likewise, those sitting in a ship, although the ship is carried along very swiftly, easily judge that the ship is at rest.
LXV.

units.la: Facilè etiam contingit ut quod quiescit id moveri sensus judicet; Ita littora, quæ præternavigamus, moveri visus frequenter judicat. Ita de nocte contingit ut intuentes lunam & nubes inter lunam & nos interpositas putemus nubes quiescere & lunam moveri; Quanquàm intellectu deprehendamus quòd lunæ motus assicere visum non possit.
units.tr: It also easily happens that the sense judges what is at rest to be moving. Thus the shores we sail past often seem to the eye to be moving. So too by night, when we look at the moon and at clouds interposed between the moon and us, we may think the clouds are at rest and the moon is moving, although by the intellect we perceive that the motion of the moon cannot affect the sight.
LXVI.

units.la: Quæris unde fiat ut quod quiescit moveri & quod movetur quiescere aliquando videatur. Resp. Id vel inde est quòd res metiri ex respectu assuevimus quem erga nos habent; Hinc fit ut quod respectu nostri situm mutat vel non mutat, id moveri vel quiescere putemus, quanquàm velocissimè moveatur; Ita navigium, quò vehimur, à nobis spectatur ut quiescens quia situm, quem respectu nostri habet, non mutat; Vice versâ fi in lectore staremus & idem navigium præterveheretur, littus quiescere & navigium moveri sensus judicaret. Vel deinde id oritur ex eo quòd alterutrum corpus pro arbitrio spectamus ut quiescens ex consuetudine,quâ in omni motu unum spectatur ut quiescens. Ita quando de nocte contingit ut luna moveri videatur, id ex eo est quòd nubem interpositam spectavimus ut quiescentem,fi verò attentionem nostram, quâ nubem spectavimus ut quiescentem, transferre volumus in lunam ut eam fpectemus ut quiescentem, tunc fiet ut nubes videatur moveri & luna quiescere.
units.tr: You ask how it happens that what is at rest seems to be moving, and what is moving seems at times to be at rest. Answer: this arises in part from our habit of measuring things by the relation they bear to us. Hence whatever changes or does not change its position relative to us, we think to be moving or at rest, even if it is moving very swiftly. Thus the ship in which we are carried is regarded by us as at rest, because it does not change the position it has relative to us; conversely, if we stood on the shore and the same ship were sailing past, the shore would seem to the sense to be at rest and the ship to be moving. Again, this arises from the fact that we arbitrarily regard one of the two bodies as at rest, by the custom by which in every motion one thing is regarded as at rest. So when it happens by night that the moon seems to be moving, this is because we regarded the interposed cloud as at rest; but if we wish to transfer our attention, by which we regarded the cloud as at rest, to the moon, so as to regard the moon as at rest, then it will come about that the cloud seems to move and the moon to be at rest.
COROLLARIA

units.la: 1. In aqua stagnante non minus est motûs quàm in aqua fluente.
units.tr: 1. In standing water there is no less motion than in flowing water.

units.la: 2. Nec plus est motûs in homine currente quàm in eodem quiescente.
units.tr: 2. There is no more motion in a man running than in the same man standing still.

units.la: 3. In corpore tardè moto potest plus esse motûs quàm in corpore celeriter moto.
units.tr: 3. In a body moving slowly there can be more motion than in a body moving quickly.

units.la: 4. In corpore moto eò est plus motûs quò plus in eo est quietis.
units.tr: 4. In a moving body there is more motion the more rest there is in it.
To the Most Distinguished Respondent, Mr.

units.la: SCANDIT in excelsam populo spectante cathedram DE LOSEA, sumos appetit atq; gradus. Plaudite Sicelides, gratantia fundite vota, Inq; caput flores spargite odoriferos. Nunc vigilando tibi palmam laurumq; parasti, Quæ magni semper signa laboris erunt. Horrendum David membris animisq; Goliam, Hostes, ut vicit, sic superare queas.
units.tr: DE LOSEA climbs into the lofty chair while the people look on, and seeks the highest steps. Applaud, Sicilian Muses, pour out grateful vows, and scatter fragrant flowers upon his head. Now by your vigils you have won the palm and the laurel, which will always be the signs of great labour. As David with his limbs and spirit overcame Goliath, so may you overcome your enemies.

units.la: Hæc paucula cognato suo perdilecto scripsit CORNELIUS SUTER.
units.tr: These few lines were written by Cornelius Suter to his most dearly beloved cousin.
FINIS
